title: Stasimon 1 (lines 324–353)

teacherSummary.text: The Chorus sings of human wonders: sailing, farming, taming animals, speech, thought and cities. Humans can solve almost everything except death. Whoever honours the laws and the gods makes the city stand; whoever departs from right becomes an outcast.

context.history: This is one of the most famous choral odes in Greek drama, praising human skill in the age of Athens' greatness.

significance: The ode is double-edged: human cleverness can serve right or wrong. Its last lines can be read against either Antigone or Creon.

They stress man's mastery over nature

The ode praises human cleverness, yet the play's clever people are already in trouble. Creon has devised a careful policy for the State, but the burial has slipped past his guards. Antigone has secretly carried out her plan, but she is caught and brought in. Cunning lets humans act boldly, but it cannot control what follows.

Both prize loyalty to the city: Creon wants citizens who put the State above friends, and the ode praises the man who honours the laws of the land. But the ode adds that the good citizen also reveres the Gods of the State. That addition opens a gap Creon has ignored, since his edict may offend the gods.

The elders praise whoever honours the laws of the land and reveres the gods, and reject whoever leaves the path of right. They do not say whose law or which gods. Both Creon, who speaks for the State, and Antigone, who speaks for the gods, can claim to be the good citizen, so the elders stay cautious and leave the judgment open.

satQuestions.passage:
Many wonders there be, but naught more wondrous than man:
Over the surging sea, with a whitening south wind wan,
Through the foam of the firth, man makes his perilous way;
And the eldest of deities Earth that knows not toil nor decay
Ever he furrows and scores, as his team, year in year out,
With breed of the yokèd horse, the ploughshare turneth about.
The light-witted birds of the air, the beasts of the weald and the wood
He traps with his woven snare, and the brood of the briny flood.
Master of cunning he: the savage bull, and the hart
Who roams the mountain free, are tamed by his infinite art;
And the shaggy rough-maned steed is broken to bear the bit.
Speech and the wind-swift speed of counsel and civic wit,
He hath learnt for himself all these; and the arrowy rain to fly
And the nipping airs that freeze, ’neath the open winter sky.
He hath provision for all: fell plague he hath learnt to endure;
Safe whate’er may befall: yet for death he hath found no cure.

anchorPassages.text:
That guide man now to the light, but now to counsels of ill.
If he honours the laws of the land, and reveres the Gods of the State
Proudly his city shall stand; but a cityless outcast I rate
Whoso bold in his pride from the path of right doth depart;
Ne’er may I sit by his side, or share the thoughts of his heart.
What strange vision meets my eyes,
Fills me with a wild surprise?
Sure I know her, sure ’tis she,
The maid Antigone.
Hapless child of hapless sire,
Didst thou recklessly conspire,
Madly brave the King’s decree?
Therefore are they haling thee?

weDoAnswers: This is one of the most famous choral odes in Greek drama, praising human skill in the age of Athens' greatness. Read closely: “If he honours the laws of the land, and reveres the Gods of the State Proudly his city shall stand; but a cityless outcast I rate Whoso bold in his pride from the path of right doth depart; Ne’er may I sit by his side, or share the thoughts of his heart.” (Chorus, lines 342–345).
analysis.weDoWords: “Honours”, “reveres” and “cityless outcast” stand out in lines 342–345. The ode ties a city’s strength to respect for both its laws and its gods, and it warns that pride can cut a person off from the community. “Cityless outcast” names that penalty in two words, set against the city that “shall stand.”

segments.script: This is one of the most famous choral odes in Greek drama, praising human skill in the age of Athens' greatness. The ode is double-edged: human cleverness can serve right or wrong. Its last lines can be read against either Antigone or Creon. Theme: The Ode on Man praises human skill and then ties a standing city to honouring both land-laws and the gods, so cleverness is judged by piety as well as power. Imagery: Sailing, ploughing, taming and speech pile up as pictures of mastery, then stop at death, the one limit no craft can cure. Structure: The ode moves from wonder at humankind to a law about the cityless outcast, so praise turns into a test that either Antigone or Creon may fail. Watch for burial and the unburied body: The ode never names the corpse, yet its outcast who departs from right hangs over the body Creon has left unburied outside the walls.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “He hath provision for all: fell plague he hath learnt to endure; / Safe whate’er may befall: yet for death he hath found no cure” slowly and put it in my own words: In these lines the Chorus reaches the end of its list of human achievements: man “hath provision for all” and has even learned to endure plague. Next, craft. I notice the turn on “yet”: every triumph in the list stops at death, since “for death he hath found no cure.” The strongest word is “provision”: the word “provision” sums up man's foresight, which makes the one thing he cannot provide for stand out. Then, effect. What do lines 338–339 reveal about the Ode on Man? My answer: Lines 338–339 reveal the ode's turning point: human skill is vast but bounded by death. That limit prepares the last stanza's warning that cleverness can lead “now to counsels of ill,” a warning that can be read against Antigone or against Creon.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Ask: What words in this line stand out, and what do they suggest? Expected student answer: “Honours”, “reveres” and “cityless outcast” stand out. The ode ties a city's strength to respect for both its laws and its gods, and it warns that pride can cut a person off from the community. Ask: How does this line connect to divine law and human law? Expected student answer: The Chorus says a city stands when a man “honours the laws of the land, and reveres the Gods of the State,” binding human law and divine reverence in one measure. (Chorus, lines 342–345.)

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the scene for theme, imagery (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about the Ode on Man? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Stasimon 1 (lines 324–353) develops the idea of the Ode on Man. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of theme and imagery shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: The ode is double-edged: human cleverness can serve right or wrong. Its last lines can be read against either Antigone or Creon. When the text says “If he honours the laws of the land, and reveres the Gods of the State / Proudly his city shall stand; but a cityless outcast I rate / Whoso bold in his pride from the path of right doth depart; / Ne’er may I sit by his side, or share the thoughts of his heart” (Stasimon 1, lines 342–345), it shows this directly. The Chorus sings of human wonders: sailing, farming, taming animals, speech, thought and cities. Humans can solve almost everything except death. Whoever honours the laws and the gods makes the city stand; whoever departs from right becomes an outcast.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The ode is double-edged: human cleverness can serve right or wrong. Its last lines can be read against either Antigone or Creon. Useful evidence: “If he honours the laws of the land, and reveres the Gods of the State / Proudly his city shall stand; but a cityless outcast I rate / Whoso bold in his pride from the path of right doth depart” (Stasimon 1, lines 342–345): Chorus, lines 342–345. On theme: The Ode on Man praises human skill and then ties a standing city to honouring both land-laws and the gods, so cleverness is judged by piety as well as power. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.
